articles.title: Iran targets US military base in Bahrain with drone attack
articles.snippet: It marks the second attack on the country in three days and comes as the US and Iran remain locked in a stand-off over the Strait of Hormuz.
articles.full_text:
Iran targets US military base in Bahrain with drone attack
- Published
Iran launched a drone attack against a US military base in Bahrain on Sunday, its second attempt to target the country in three days.
The country's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said it targeted the US air defence radar facility at al-Riffa air base in Bahrain using six drones.
Bahrain's military said its air defence systems intercepted and destroyed the Iranian air attacks "before they could achieve their objectives".
It comes after Iran fired drones at Bahrain on Friday, its first attack against Gulf countries since September.
The US and Iran are locked in a stand-off over the Strait of Hormuz. About a fifth of the world's gas and oil supply usually flows through it but shipping has been restricted since the outbreak of war in February.
Iran insists that it should control the strait and has been attacking what it calls "unauthorised" traffic, while the US military is providing protection for tankers shuttling oil through the strait to keep exports flowing from Gulf Arab states.
As sirens sounded across Bahrain on Sunday the interior ministry called on citizens to head to their nearest safe location.
Bahrain's foreign ministry said: "The Kingdom of Bahrain condemns in the strongest terms the continued brutal Iranian attacks on its territory and holds Iran fully responsible for their consequences."
In a statement on the strikes shared by Iran's state broadcaster on Telegram, the IRGC said: "The Strait of Hormuz is closed, and any aggression by the American enemy will be met with an even harsher and more forceful response."
Earlier this week, the IRGC claimed that it struck a US early warning radar system in Bahrain on Friday.
The US military has denied the claim, stating that the IRGC launched two one-way attack drones towards Bahrain and both were shot down by US forces. It added that there were no injuries or damage.
Earlier in the week the US carried out strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, US officials told CBS, the BBC's US partner.
The officials described the strikes as limited and defensive, and said they were in response to the IRGC firing on a US aircraft.
Iranian state news agency Irna reported explosions on Qeshm on Monday. The IRGC did not comment but said its forces had shot down two US MQM-170 drones south of the island and a US MQ-9 drone east of the Strait.
The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated a naval blockade of Iranian ports.
Iranian negotiators had been discussing with mediators a proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days if the US meets seven conditions, reportedly including the lifting of the naval blockade and releasing frozen Iranian assets.
However this week Donald Trump said that the US was no longer interested in a deal to end the war with Iran and ordered Vice-President JD Vance, who had been involved in efforts to restart negotiations, to focus on domestic US politics.

articles.title: Three men sentenced to death in Jordan over fatal church mass shooting
articles.snippet: The attack on funeral at a Greek Orthodox church killed nine and injured 34 others last month.
articles.full_text:
Three men sentenced to death in Jordan over fatal church mass shooting
- Published
A Jordanian court has sentenced three men to death by hanging for carrying out a fatal mass shooting on a church last month.
The attack on 23 October killed nine people and injured 34 others who had been attending a Christian funeral at a Greek Orthodox church in Karak governorate.
Jordan's Armed Forces said in a statement on Sunday that the men had been convicted of committing "terrorist acts", as well as possessing weapons, "promoting the ideas of a terrorist organisation" and "conspiracy to commit terrorist acts".
The three men - two Jordanian brothers and their brother-in-law - fled the scene of the attack and were arrested three days later. They have not been publicly identified.
Karak is home to a sizeable Christian community in the Muslim-majority kingdom.
CCTV footage from the day of the attack showed three men holding guns approaching and firing on St George's church in the village of Hmoud.
A second video showed dead and wounded people lying on the ground amid chaotic scenes at the church.
It is still unclear why the attackers chose to target that specific church.
Shortly after the attack, Jordan's King Abdullah II wrote on X: "The terrorist attack against Karak will be met with the harshest retaliation.
"Those who delude themselves into thinking that they can divide Jordanians with their bullets have no chance in the face of our unity."
The three men fled the scene of the shooting and were later located inside an abandoned house in Karak governorate, south of the capital, Amman.
They refused to surrender and opened fire on security forces, who returned fire and wounded all three of them, the Public Security Directorate said at the time. No security personnel were hurt in the shootout.
King Abdullah praised security forces for chasing the suspects "to the very end".
The week after the Karak shooting, Jordan struck what its military said were "terrorist organisations" in Syria in retaliation to the church attack.
Syrian health officials told state media that five people, including women, children and an elderly man, were killed in the strike on a village in the southern Daraa province. Jordan said its fighter jets had killed and wounded "several terrorists" without giving further details.
Jordan said it had co-ordinated with the Syrian government, but Syria said it had not been notified in advance.
Executions in Jordan are carried out by hanging. The kingdom previously observed an unofficial ban on executions from 2006 to 2014, and another pause from 2017 until June this year.

articles.title: South Korea's top scorer in tax accountancy exam admits cheating
articles.snippet: Han Won-seok, 34, confessed to using a hidden camera and AI to get a near-perfect mark on the significant test.
articles.full_text:
South Korea's top scorer in tax accountancy exam admits cheating
- Published
A candidate who came first in South Korea's certified tax accountancy exam has admitted cheating by using a miniature camera, mobile phone and AI tools.
Han Won-seok confessed in a video on the YouTube account of his lawyer, Lee Don-Ho, adding that he had confessed to the Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency and offered details on how he cheated.
The 34-year-old scored 397.5 out of 400 points in the first round, getting just one of 160 questions wrong, which initially raised suspicions and sparked online speculation.
Standardised national tests play an outsized role in career trajectories for South Koreans, making their results - and efforts to unduly inflate those results - of great importance.
"I cheated in both the first and second rounds of the tax account exam by using electronic devices and generative AI," Han said in the video published on Sunday.
"I used a microcamera to photograph the test questions and sent them to an AI then checked my answers on my smartphone to commit the cheating."
When accusations he had cheated first began to surface, Han had denied any wrongdoing - but said he had changed his mind after thinking about the feelings of the candidate who had come second in the exam.
He went on to apologise to the other entrants who had passed the tests fairly.
"It seems that because of me, other successful candidates are being suspected," he suggested.
The Ministry of Employment and Labour and the Human Resources Development Service held an emergency meeting after Han admitted cheating.
The South Korean president's policy chief Ha Jun-kyung said new measures would be introduced to prevent cheating and warned "past crimes" would be "tracked down and apprehended to the very end".
Those found to have used AI to cheat in the tax accountancy exam will have their qualification revoked and will be banned from retaking the test for five years, the government said.
The scandal comes just days before the east Asian nation's annual college entrance exam, a crucial hurdle for students.
Can smart glasses exam cheating be stopped?
Asia Specific
A series of cases involving exam cheating with AI glasses in South Korea has universities and schools scrambling to rein in the use of the technology.
Han said he had only cheated to try and earn money and get a job that would make his parents proud of him again.
Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency told Korean news agency Yonhap on Sunday that it was looking into the case.
"We received a written confession through the test taker's lawyer this morning regarding cheating on the tax accountant exam," it confirmed in a statement.
It added that the case had now been assigned to investigators.
Because of the significance of the national exams, instances of cheating are not uncommon in South Korea, and cases involving the use of AI have become more prominent as the technology becomes more sophisticated.
Last month, two college applicants were reported to have used AI glasses to try and cheat their entrance exams at two Seoul universities.
Education ministry data also says there were four cases of cheating through AI glasses at middle and high schools in the past 12 months.

articles.title: Suspected China spy linked to Nvidia's ex-boss left in 2025, Megaspeed says
articles.snippet: The Nvidia scandal has raised questions over whether advanced AI chips ended up in China, despite US restrictions.
articles.full_text:
Suspected China spy linked to Nvidia's ex-boss left in 2025, Megaspeed says
- Published
Alice Huang, a suspected China spy who has been linked to Nvidia's former boss Jensen Huang, left her executive role at Megaspeed in August last year, the company says.
Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive of the AI chip-making giant Nvidia after it emerged he had allegedly had affairs with Alice Huang as well as with one of his employees.
Megaspeed is the biggest buyer of Nvidia chips in south-east Asia and the scandal at Nvidia has raised questions about the possibility that high-end AI chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions.
The Singapore-based company said on Sunday it had launched an internal investigation into its business.
It said it was aware of reports "containing assertions about our business, supply chain and global operations that are not supported by verifiable evidence".
It added that it "conducts legitimate and lawful business" and has "retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation".
On Friday, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blamed fellow Trump cabinet colleague Howard Lutnick's commerce department for failing to properly oversee the export of high-end chips.
Bessent told CNBC that several agencies "were in favour of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months... but Commerce has the pen... and you will have to ask them about their internal process".
The so-called entity list restricts US trade with overseas firms and individuals.
Lutnick has been called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over his department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips.
Other congressional committees have asked both Lutnick and his department to retain all records relating to Nvidia and Jensen Huang.
Megaspeed is suspected of giving backdoor access to Nvidia chips to Chinese companies via its data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand.
Nvidia has been banned from selling its advanced chips to China.
While Singapore does not prohibit the transfer of advanced AI chips to companies abroad, such moves can breach US export controls.
Singapore has said that while it does not enforce "unilateral export controls imposed by other countries" it expects all companies in its jurisdiction to respect such regulations.
Megaspeed said it "designs and maintains its global operational and supply-chain control frameworks to comply with all applicable laws and regulatory regimes". It said this includes "US export control requirements and local jurisdiction rules in every market where we operate".
China has denied that Alice Huang is a spy and warned the US not to use the scandal as a "pretext for imposing a technological blockade" on AI technology.

articles.title: Israel kills Hamas commander in strike on Gaza camp, officials say
articles.snippet: Both Hamas and IDF officials confirm the death of Samir Abu Younis, commander of the Rafah Brigade.
articles.full_text:
Israel kills Hamas commander in strike on Gaza camp, officials say
- Published
A senior Hamas figure who helped plan and oversee the 7 October 2023 attack on Israel has been killed in an Israeli airstrike, officials in Israel and Gaza have said.
Samir Abu Younis, the newly appointed commander of the Rafah Brigade, was killed on Saturday in Al-Mawasi in the southern Gaza Strip, according to Hamas's Al-Qassam Brigades military wing.
A local Hamas official confirmed Younis's death. The Israeli military said it had targeted him and that prior to the strike "steps were taken to mitigate harm to civilians".
Eyewitnesses in Gaza said four missiles struck a tent in the Al-Waha camp, which shelters hundreds of displaced people in Al-Mawasi, causing a fire to break out.
A medical source at Nasser Hospital in the southern city of Khan Younis said three injured people had arrived there, as well as a dead body.
The Israel Defence Forces (IDF) and Israel's security agency, the ISA, confirmed in a statement on Telegram that it had "eliminated" Younis.
Describing him as a "central figure among Hamas's senior figures", it said he had "acted with the aim of trying to restore the strength of the brigade and the Hamas terrorist organisation".
It added: "Younis directed the brigade's terrorists to advance and carry out terror attacks against Israeli civilians and IDF troops."
Al-Qassam Brigades wrote on Telegram that Younis had "participated in numerous high-profile operations and resisted enemy incursions", and was "one of the most important commanders involved in planning and overseeing the 7 October attack".
It described his killing as a "cowardly assassination".
Younis, 53, had been in his position since 15 September, following the death of the brigade's previous commander, Nael Abu Obeid.
He joined Hamas' armed wing in 1991 and held several senior operational roles before becoming commander. His funeral will be held on Sunday afternoon in Khan Younis, Hamas said.
The Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed an 251 others taken hostage, triggered the most recent war in Gaza.
Since then, more than 74,650 people have been killed in the Palestinian territory, the health ministry there says.
Though a ceasefire was reached last October, Israel has continued strikes it says are targeting remaining Hamas militants, which it argues it has the right to do under the terms of the ceasefire agreement.
More than 1,640 people have been killed in Gaza since the October 2025 ceasefire, according to the territory's health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.

articles.title: Czechs rally against plan to switch funding of public media
articles.snippet: Protesters say the move will stifle media freedom, while the government insists broadcasters need to cut costs.
articles.full_text:
Czechs rally against plan to switch funding of public media
- Published
Thousands of people have gathered in central Prague to protest against the Czech government's plans to scrap the licence fee and use the state budget to fund public media.
Critics say the plans would allow politicians to stifle media freedom.
The coalition government - which consists of the populist ANO party and two right-wing Eurosceptic parties - insists the change will not affect editorial independence, but wants broadcasters to cut costs.
Parliament passed the first draft of the proposal late last month. Since then, thousands of Czechs have taken part in protests.
Czech households currently pay â 205 crowns ($9.44; Â£7.06) a month for TV and radio.
Sunday's protest was organised by the Million Moments for Democracy association which said "roughly 400,000" people had attended.
It is being described as the largest protest since the Czech Republic's independence in 1993.
"I know that our entire Czech Television is a guarantee of truth and objectivity," pensioner Milana Rudolfova, 72, told Reuters news agency.
"If we do not have public television and radio then unfortunately we will not be able to believe anything anymore."
Prime Minister Andrej Babis has insisted the government does not want to control public media.
"The funding system is changing, no one wants to control public media, no one wants to dictate to them what they should say and do, no one wants to nationalise them," Babis told the Czech News Agency.
"We are doing this because the system is already outdated and most of Europe is going the same way today and others are joining in," he added.
Some European countries, including France and Norway, have moved away from the public licence fee model in the last few years.
France removed it in 2022 and its public media, which also carries advertising, is now funded by a portion of the income from VAT.
Norway abolished its license fee in 2020 and moved its public broadcaster's funding into the national budget.
Some protesters wore pointed hats folded out of newspapers as a tribute to an animated character, Vecernicek, who has introduced Czech Television's nightly children's bedtime stories for decades.
Critics have compared the government's media bill to changes in Hungary under former Prime Minister Viktor OrbÃ¡n, who tightly controlled state media when he was in power.
Prime Minister Andrej Babis was appointed in December in 2025, and has faced criticism over his coalition's attacks on Czech media.
"Political attacks against private and public media have become one of the hallmarks of Andrej Babis' premiership," said Pavol Szalai, Prague Bureau director of international press freedom organisation Reporters Without Borders, in June.

Critics say proposed funding changes will give government more control of state media.
Tens of thousands of people have taken to the streets of the Czech capital to protest against proposed changes to the funding of public service media, which critics fear could weaken broadcaster independence.
Many of the protesters assembled in Letna Park in Prague on Sunday afternoon.

Some of the demonstrators wore pointed hats folded out of newspapers in tribute to an animated character who has introduced Czech Television’s nightly children’s bedtime stories for decades.
Local authorities anticipated a large crowd days before the November 17 holiday commemorating the 1989 Velvet Revolution against Communist rule, which propelled dissident playwright Vaclav Havel to power.
Under the proposed changes introduced last month, the government of billionaire Prime Minister Andrej Babis wants to replace the current monthly fee of 205 crowns ($9.45), which is charged to each household, with funding from the state budget.
Opponents say the change will stifle media freedom as it will make the outlets more dependent on the state. The government insists the plan will not affect editorial independence or programme content.
The bill has passed a preliminary vote in parliament and awaits further debate.
Broadcast workers have been striking against the proposal since June and earlier this month public media employees staged a one-day strike, leading to state media boycotts by artists and students.
The Million Moments for Democracy group organised Sunday’s demonstration and said “Babis and his government obviously think they will get away with anything… that they can ignore experts, silence critics and treat democratic institutions like their property”.
The group said the protest might be “the largest public gathering in Czech history”, as organisers expect 400,000 to 600,000 demonstrators.
Although trust in the media is low – about 30 percent to 33 percent according to the latest Reuters Institute Digital News Report – public service journalism is among the most trusted news sources in the country, with Czech Television the most-watched broadcaster across several age groups.
The proposed media reform has attracted international attention: the European Broadcasting Union, the European Federation of Journalists, Reporters Without Borders and the International Press Institute have all criticised it.

articles.title: Fifth Canadian soldier dies from injuries caused by large fire at military base
articles.snippet: Pte William Douglas Dal Bianco died from his injuries on Friday, a month after a fire that tore through CFB Wainwright.
articles.full_text:
Fifth Canadian soldier dies from injuries caused by large fire at military base
- Published
A fifth Canadian soldier has died from injuries he suffered when a grass fire swept through a military training area last month.
Four people were killed initially and dozens were injured when the fire, which ignited during a live fire training exercise, spread rapidly through Canadian Forces Base Wainwright carried by strong winds on 17 October.
Pte William Douglas Dal Bianco, who had been receiving medical care in Ontario, died on Friday, the Canadian Armed Forces said in a statement.
Prime Minister Mark Carney wrote on X: "Canadians are holding Private Dal Bianco's loved ones, and all those still grieving in the wake of this terrible tragedy, in our hearts."
The Canadian Armed Forces said that 24 military personnel were still in hospital receiving treatment, while 14 had been released as of Saturday. Thirty-eight military personnel had been injured in total.
Members of 1 Canadian Mechanized Brigade Group had been conducting live-fire training at the base, in the province of Alberta, when the fire broke out.
Military officials said at the time that the fire spread across a kilometre in a matter of seconds, taking many of those on the base by surprise.
Firefighters battled the blaze through the night, while nearby hospitals became inundated by injured personnel and staff.
Carney described it as "one of the worst tragedies for the forces on Canadian soil in peacetime".
An investigation found that the fire was likely sparked by a grenade launcher being fired on the base's grenade range, officials said.
Firefighters on the base had known about the fire but could not tackle it because it was in a danger area that could contain unspent explosives.
Canadian Chief of the Defence Staff Gen Jennie Carignan said the nation's armed forces were "heartbroken" by the loss of Dal Bianco, while Defence Minister David McGuinty offered his "deepest condolences" to his family, friends and colleagues.
"No words can ease the pain of losing a loved one, and my thoughts remain with all those affected by this tragedy," he said.
"We remain committed to supporting the families and the Canadian Armed Forces community during this profoundly difficult time, and to honouring Private Dal Bianco's service, dedication and sacrifice to Canada."

articles.title: Judge blocks Trump closure of 'Trash Island' Washington DC golf course on Sunday
articles.snippet: The temporary order is part of a months-long challenge to the US president's plans to upgrade East Potomac Golf Links into a championship course.
articles.full_text:
Judge blocks Trump closure of 'Trash Island' Washington DC golf course on Sunday
- Published
A federal judge has temporarily blocked the US government's closure of an historic golf course and park in Washington DC.
US District Judge Ana Reyes has been overseeing a months-long challenge to the president's plans for East Potomac Golf Links, which he said would be closed from 15 November for extensive renovations.
Reyes has said President Donald Trump cannot close the park nor its golf course, but added that his administration was not required to actively manage either.
Trump, an avid golfer, has said his plans to upgrade the 106-year-old course will create "one of the Best and Most Spectacular Golf Courses anywhere in the World". The BBC has contacted the White House for comment.
Declaring the current course "Trash Island", he announced in October that it would be renovated over 15 months to create a space that "will be open to the Public while, at the same time, designed to the Highest Level of Golf and able to hold World Class Tournaments" - despite the ongoing litigation.
Reyes said in a 30-page decision issued on Saturday that the Trump administration's justifications for the proposed course closures were pretextual and that the government had violated at least two federal laws "to meet an arbitrary deadline".
"The government proposes to close a historic park, daily enjoyed by Washingtonians of all stripes, indefinitely," Reyes wrote.
She said the closure "runs counter to the public interest in utilising national parkland", adding that the government had not "plausibly identified any harm it would suffer from a temporary restraining order that preserves the status quo pending further proceedings".
Her order will last until 28 November.
A coalition of advocacy and legal groups opposing the closure and renovation said they are "grateful that the court has stopped the government from unlawfully closing East Potomac Park and depriving people of this priceless piece of American history and wonderful recreation space".
"Our laws prevent this administration from acting without a fair and public process, and today's order will stop the government from ignoring those laws," said the coalition, which represents the plaintiffs and includes Democracy Forward and the Democracy Defenders Fund. "We are eager to continue to argue this case in court."
The legal dispute dates back to February, when the DC Preservation League and others sued over redevelopment plans for the park.
The historic course, which sits two miles (3km) south of the White House, is one of three public courses run by the National Park Service (NPS) in the nation's capital.
The legal fight then escalated in October when the NPS began to cut down hundreds of trees without notifying Reyes until 15 hours before work was set to begin.
After the trees were cut, Reyes ordered the Trump administration to stop tree removal until at least 26 October and give her three business days' notice about making any other permanent changes.
Despite the work stoppage, Trump announced that the course would be closed for 15 months from 15 November to accommodate for the renovations. He also shared a rendering of the course redesign.
"The current Course is old, broken, dilapidated and of no further use or effect. It is in very poor condition, with falling, dangerous and disease-infested trees and, importantly, a collapsing and hazardous seawall," he said in a post on Truth Social.
Reyes has since separately opened an inquiry into whether justice department attorneys had "made misrepresentations to the court and otherwise violated ethical rules".
That included whether giving late notice to the court about the renovation plans had been "done in bad faith", and whether the attorneys failed to correct previously false statements or withheld information.
She said she would carry out the inquiry with a special master, an independent third party.

Somalia: We would not have recovered without the international community
Somalia continues to face al-Shabab rebellion and political friction, leading officials to urge international support.
Somalia’s State Minister for Foreign Affairs Ali Mohamed Omar says Somalia has come a long way since its government collapsed 30 years ago, plunging the country into civil war.
Omar notes that Somalia would not have recovered without the international community’s help.
The United Nations established a political office to help rebuild institutions and resolve political disputes. And more than three decades after its creation, the mission ended in October at the request of the government, which says it wants to be responsible for its own affairs.
But the government will face challenges. African Union peacekeepers are still on the ground supporting Mogadishu in its fight against al-Shabaab, an armed group linked to al-Qaeda that controls large parts of central and southern Somalia. Cuts to United States funding threaten the African Union’s mission.
Meanwhile, Somalia’s opposition says its president is not legitimate, as the government says the new constitution allows him to stay in office until next year.
Omar says that despite these issues, Somalia is more stable than it was a few years ago. And he hopes the international community will continue supporting it financially as it seeks to become a stronger state.

articles.source: Al Jazeera – Breaking News, World News and Video from Al Jazeera
articles.snippet: Iraq has dismantled an alleged smuggling ring in Jurf al-Sakhar which could squeeze militias and avert internal strife
articles.full_text:
Will Iraq’s oil smuggling crackdown disarm militias without a conflict?
Iraq has dismantled an alleged smuggling ring in Jurf al-Sakhar which could financially squeeze militias and avert internal strife.
The Iraqi government has launched a sweeping anticorruption crackdown centred on the Jurf al-Sakhar area, a stronghold of Iran-linked militias near Baghdad.
The campaign has seen the dismissal and judicial referral of nine senior officials accused of corruption. It has also led to the sacking of top security directors, the Babil police chief and the director of the Oil Pipelines Company at the Ministry of Oil.
Recommended Stories

- list 2 of 3Iraq parliament approves al-Zaidi’s cabinet amid growing economic concerns
- list 3 of 3Iraq PM sacks nine officials over oil smuggling in pro-Iran stronghold
While officially framed as an initiative to protect public funds from a widespread smuggling network, analysts believe the move is a highly calculated strategy to sever the financial arteries of armed factions that refuse to integrate into the state apparatus.
At the heart of this confrontation is Jurf al-Sakhar – also known as Jurf al-Nasr – a stronghold of the Kataib Hezbollah group, believed to have close links to Iran.
For over a decade, Jurf al-Nasr has allegedly harboured illicit oil refineries. An intelligence report released last week claimed that the area was at the centre of a major corruption scheme involving oil revenues and Iran-linked militias.
That led Iraq’s Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi to launch the crackdown, with an Iraqi security committee entering Jurf al-Nasr on Friday to investigate, following the arrest of other officials accused of graft. The formerly Sunni-majority area has long been considered outside government control since Iraqi militias seized the area a decade ago.
Michael Knights, head of MENA research at Horizon Engage, told Al Jazeera that Jurf al-Sakhar’s value is deeply rooted in recent developments in Iraq, when Iran-linked militias used the campaign against ISIL (ISIS) to stamp their authority in the country.
“Iran-backed militias illegally seized and renamed Jurf al-Sakr when they conducted sectarian cleansing of the Sunni residents in the area in 2014, under the cover of the anti-Daesh [ISIL] war,” Knights explained.
The town, about 60km (37 miles) from Baghdad, is at a critical point near the Shia pilgrimage route between the Iraqi capital and Karbala.
It was once the site of Saddam Hussein’s military industrial complexes, which made Jurf al-Nasr an ideal place for Iraqi militias to test, build and hide rockets, drones and missiles, said Knights.
“If full control is taken, which is unlikely, the government would be able to finally tell Iraqis that a militia had been removed from its base and the legal residents of the area allowed to return,” he said. “This would be like taking back the Bekaa Valley from Hezbollah.”
Knights said the actual financial impact on Kataib Hezbollah of the Jurf al-Sakhar crackdown could be less spectacular than expected, with the militia having other sources of revenue.
Analysts say that dismantling the smuggling networks is part of a wider project to bring weapons under the control of the state.
After some Iran-linked militias missed a deadline to disarm this year, PM al-Zaidi now appears to be using economic pressure to weaken these armed groups without directly confronting them.
Security and strategic expert Saif Raad told Al Jazeera that the anticorruption campaign in Jurf al-Sakhar is essentially a message from the PM that no group is above the law.
“This duality is over. Part of what happened now is that the Iraqi people knew these factions and knew why they hold onto weapons, and I believe this is a victory achieved by the government without a single drop of Iraqi blood,” Raad said.
“Jurf al-Sakhar has been around for, let’s say, more than ten years; for ten years no prime minister was able to enter this area.”
Averting armed conflict
A central focus of the government’s strategy is executing this crackdown without igniting a potentially explosive ‘Shia-on-Shia’ armed conflict.
The militia network which emerged following the US-led invasion of Iraq – and was emboldened during the campaign against ISIL – includes groups with widely divergent political and religious views. Some are closely aligned to Iran and accused of being proxies of Tehran, while others are closer to the federal government.
In a bid to prevent violence, Al-Zaidi reportedly cooperated with leaders of the Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF), particularly with the Badr Organisation, before initiating the arrests and dismissals in Jurf al-Sakhar, Raad said.
Fadel Abu Ragheef, an Iraqi political analyst, told Al Jazeera that leveraging Hadi al-Amiri, leader of the Badr Organisation, was essential to neutralising the threat from the militias.
“The Badr Organisation is considered the largest combat force within the Popular Mobilisation Forces, so the process of focusing on this issue… is a fundamental part of strengthening the state project,” Raad observed.
“[The campaign] is a major shift in the process of strengthening the state and state institutions and making the Popular Mobilisation Forces an active and large part in controlling these groups [militias outside government control].”
Political analyst Ali Fadhlallah said that due to the structural nature of Iraq’s political and religious leadership, an internal war between the Shia factions was never likely to break out, particularly due to the influence Grand Ayatollah Ali al-Sistani.
“The Shia component has very many large and positive factors that serve as a brake for any clash that is supposed to happen,” Fadhlallah said.
“The presence of the rational religious authority, which has always controlled the rhythm of the political process at dangerous crossroads, definitely has a very large role and it is monitoring the events… the issue of a [Shia-Shia] clash is unlikely, even in the most difficult and miserable circumstances.”

articles.title: 20 years of Al Jazeera English: Our story is still being written
articles.source: Al Jazeera – Breaking News, World News and Video from Al Jazeera
articles.snippet: As we celebrate our 20th anniversary, we remain committed to our values and the quality of our journalism.
articles.full_text:
20 years of Al Jazeera English: Our story is still being written
As we celebrate our 20th anniversary, we remain committed to our values, the quality of our journalism and a willingness to evolve.
Twenty years ago today, on November 15, 2006, Al Jazeera English began broadcasting with a belief that the world needed a different perspective on the news. A perspective that would bring underreported stories to international attention and give people everywhere a greater opportunity to be seen and heard.
As we celebrate our 20th anniversary, that belief remains as important as ever.
The world has changed enormously over the past two decades. We have witnessed wars, political upheavals, economic crises, technological revolutions and profound changes in how people consume information. Through it all, Al Jazeera English has sought to do more than report events. We have worked to explain why they matter, explore their impact on people’s lives and help audiences understand an increasingly complex world.
Our journey has never simply been about building another international news channel. It has been about broadening the global conversation.
A different perspective on the world
From the beginning, Al Jazeera English sought to broaden international news coverage by bringing greater diversity of perspectives, voices and stories to audiences around the world.
We believed that events everywhere deserved attention, depth and serious journalism, regardless of where they took place. We also believed that people experiencing conflict, injustice, poverty and political change should not be merely subjects of news coverage, but voices within it.
This approach has helped define our editorial identity. It reflects our belief that no single perspective can fully explain our world, and that good journalism must question assumptions, examine different viewpoints and bring important stories to light.
At the heart of this philosophy is a simple principle: every human life matters, and every story deserves to be approached with dignity and fairness.
The people who made it possible
Behind every broadcast, investigation, documentary and breaking news story are people whose dedication makes our work possible.
Al Jazeera English brings together colleagues representing 78 nationalities, reflecting the diversity of cultures, experiences and perspectives that make our channel unique.
I think particularly of our journalists working in difficult and sometimes dangerous circumstances, often far from their families, determined to tell stories the world needs to hear.
I also think of the many colleagues working behind the scenes, whose contributions may not always be visible to audiences but remain essential to everything we achieve.
We must remember those who helped build this channel over the past two decades, including colleagues who are no longer with us. Their dedication and sacrifices are part of our history.
Our greatest achievement is not any single programme, interview or award. It is the collective effort of generations of people who have believed in the purpose of this channel.
Journalism in a changing world
The media landscape is changing at an extraordinary pace. Audiences have more choice than ever before, but also face an overwhelming volume of information, misinformation and competing narratives. Artificial intelligence is transforming how content is produced and distributed, while traditional viewing habits continue to evolve.
These developments present challenges, but also opportunities.
We must embrace innovation, explore new storytelling formats and meet audiences wherever they choose to engage with news. But technological progress must never come at the expense of what makes journalism valuable.
Technology cannot replace editorial judgement, human understanding, compassion or the responsibility to establish what is true.
Credibility is earned through consistent, rigorous journalism. Trust takes years to build and can be lost quickly. Neither should ever be taken for granted.
The next chapter
Today, as we celebrate our 20th anniversary, Al Jazeera English also unveils a new on-air look, marking the beginning of another chapter in our journey. But our ambitions extend well beyond what audiences see on their screens.
We want to strengthen our journalism, deepen our storytelling, develop fresh ideas and engage meaningfully with audiences around the world.
Equally important is building a workplace culture based on respect, trust, fairness, openness, collaboration and accountability. A place where people feel valued, ideas are welcomed and everyone has an opportunity to contribute and grow.
Great journalism requires talented people. Sustaining it requires an environment where they can do their best work.
Twenty years is a significant milestone, but not a destination.
We should be proud of what Al Jazeera English has achieved, while recognising that our continued relevance must be earned every day through the quality of our journalism, the strength of our values and our willingness to evolve.
The world still needs journalism that questions power, challenges assumptions, brings neglected stories to light and places humanity at the centre of its reporting.
That was our promise in 2006. Twenty years later, it remains our responsibility.
Our first 20 years have shaped who we are. What we do next will define who we become.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

articles.title: Record number of migrants arrive in Spain’s Canary Islands
articles.source: Al Jazeera – Breaking News, World News and Video from Al Jazeera
articles.snippet: New EU migration and asylum laws have largely failed to stem flow of migrants to Spain and its territories.
articles.full_text:
Record number of migrants arrive in Spain’s Canary Islands
New European Union migration and asylum laws have largely failed to stem the flow of migrants to Spain and its territories.
Spain has declared a migration emergency in the Canary Islands after the arrival of more than 9,000 people in its Atlantic Ocean territory since the start of November.
Spain’s Maritime Rescue Service said it had rescued 1,488 migrants aboard 14 dinghies, also known as pirogues, most of whom arrived on El Hierro in the Canary Islands from West Africa on Saturday.
Recommended Stories

- list 2 of 3More than 300 migrants rescued off Spain’s Canary Islands
- list 3 of 3Migrants risk deadly route to Spain’s Canary Islands
That’s broken the record of 1,461 people rescued six years earlier in November 2020.
Spain’s Territorial Policy Minister Angel Victor Torres is visiting El Hierro on Sunday to discuss the surge in migrant arrivals.
Al Jazeera’s Bernard Smith, reporting from El Hierro, said the arrival this year has set a record in the 32 years since statistics have been collected.
“There’s been even more arrivals by Sunday afternoon”, Smith said, adding that the new arrivals are processed at the port in El Hierro and taken to a reception centre and sent on to other Canary Islands or to the Spanish mainland.
The European Union’s new Pact on Migration and Asylum officially came into force on June 12, 2026, introducing “firm and fair rules” for accepting asylum requests, marking the most sweeping overhaul of EU asylum and border laws in decades.
“EU states are under pressure to do more to control migration from Africa and from outside the European Union,” Smith said, adding that the new rules haven’t stopped the flow of migrants to Spain and its enclaves.
Spain’s Ceuta enclave
Last month, Spain deported more than a dozen of the 80,000 people who had entered its North African enclave of Ceuta from Morocco over a 48-hour period in late July.
At least 100 people died during the mass crossing into the autonomous city, which covers just 18.5 square kilometres (7.1sq miles) and has a population of about 80,000.
Most of the migrants arriving in El Hierro depart from West Africa, many leaving from Senegal, with hopes of reaching mainland Europe.
But to get there, they risk their lives in small, often overcrowded boats at sea.
One boat on Saturday was carrying 240 people, including 12 women and 36 children, authorities said.
The International Organization for Migration (IOM) recorded at least 450 deaths on the Western African Atlantic route in the first 10 months of 2026.
“It is a treacherous journey,” said Al Jazeera’s Nicolas Haque, reporting from Dakar in Senegal, from where some of the boats depart, adding that favourable weather conditions in the Atlantic Ocean have made departures from the coastlines in Africa much easier in recent years.
“So when the weather conditions allow it, the boats go out there,” he said, noting that migrants use “wooden fishing vessels called pirogues” in which up to 100 people are packed in for “a journey that can last one week”.

articles.title: US Air Force adopts new Force Design focusing on sensors and autonomy
articles.snippet: The Air Force's new Force Design 2026 outlines a shift toward artificial intelligence, autonomy and integrated sensors to counter emerging threats.
articles.full_text:
The U.S. Air Force has changed its strategic outlook, announcing a new Force Design 2026 that replaces its previous standards established in 2024.
“The U.S. Air Force Force Design 2026 provides an enduring framework for identifying operational problems, shaping capability development, and informing modernization priorities – ensuring the Air Force evolves how it fights, and that it fields a winning force,” an Air Force spokesperson told Military Times.
“The Force Design is a classified document so there is no releasable copy,” the spokesperson said.
In October 2024, the service announced it would follow guidance set out in a “One Force Design” document, signed by then-Chief of Staff Gen. David Allvin and said to be the “North Star” for Air Force modernization plans.
It introduced three distinct mission areas, effectively divvying up air defenses against unmanned aircraft systems. The Air Force’s drone-killing capabilities were classified in the 2024 document in categories of short-range, long-range and intercontinental defense, respectively.
Although the new Force Design 2026 document is classified, the service’s release hints at some key changes.
The new strategic outlook is said to be “more sharply articulating the need for change, and the capabilities the Air Force needs” to defeat sophisticated technology.
It lists sensors, networks and artificial intelligence as having had a rapid impact on air defenses.
“New technologies are enabling fantastic capabilities that were unimaginable just a few years ago, but those same technologies threaten some of the ways we have historically generated airpower,” Lt. Gen. Chris Niemi, deputy chief of staff for Force Modernization and Chief Modernization Officer, said in the release.
In another nod to where air defense is going, the document also notes that the “future Air Force” will seek to integrate autonomy, sensors and command and control with aircraft to “generate effects,” with a particular emphasis on being able to perform synchronously in denied environments.
In other words, a new focus on sensors and software is at play rather than on intercepting and destroying individual drones.
Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. Ken Wilsbach said in the service’s statement that the new Force Design “presents a fundamental shift” in the Air Force’s approach.
“New technologies are enabling fantastic capabilities that were unimaginable just a few years ago, but those same technologies threaten some of the ways we have historically generated airpower,” Wilsbach said.

articles.title: Judges close part of ICC Afghanistan investigations that could look at US troops
articles.snippet: The International Criminal Court will close investigations into Afghanistan that previously looked at alleged crimes by U.S. troops and focus only on actions of the Taliban.
articles.full_text:
Judges at the International Criminal Court have issued a decision to formally close part of the prosecutor’s investigations into Afghanistan that previously looked at alleged crimes by U.S. troops and to focus only on actions of the Taliban since 2021, court documents show.
The decision by the chamber formally closes not only the line of inquiry into alleged crimes by U.S. troops, which had already lain dormant since 2021, but also a probe into the Islamic State Khorasan (ISIS-K) militia. The office of the prosecutor told Reuters on Friday it had appealed the decision but could not give further details.
It is the latest step in a legal tussle between prosecutors and judges about the Afghanistan case, and comes after the United States issued institutional sanctions against the court, citing U.S. opposition to arrest warrants issued for Israeli officials and the investigation into actions of U.S. soldiers in Afghanistan.
This year, judges ordered prosecutors to split their Afghanistan inquiries into two separate probes — one focusing on the alleged crimes committed by the Taliban since 2021, and the other on the original Afghanistan inquiry, which also looked at alleged war crimes by U.S. troops but has shifted towards looking at the ISIS-K militia.
Judges said they had taken the decision to close part of the case because prosecutors had not shown they would be able to effectively investigate allegations in Afghanistan apart from the Taliban probe. The splitting of the cases means the arrest warrants issued against four Afghan Taliban leaders remain in effect.
It is unclear if formally closing part of the Afghanistan case will be enough to allay American fears over the court exerting jurisdiction over U.S. nationals, as it does not change the court’s founding statute. The statute says the court can prosecute anyone accused of atrocity crimes committed on the territory of ICC member states.

articles.title: Italy boosts GCAP fighter spending as Army vehicles take a hit in budget
articles.snippet: Italy has hiked its spending on the GCAP fighter this year while reducing funding for new army tanks and fighting vehicles, newly released spending documents have revealed.
articles.full_text:
ROME — Italy has hiked its spending on the GCAP fighter this year while reducing funding for new army tanks and fighting vehicles, newly released spending documents have revealed.
Rome has spent €875 million ($970 million) in 2026 on GCAP – the program for a sixth-generation fighter which teams Italy with the United Kingdom and Japan.
That is up on last year’s €625 million and far higher than the €275 million that planners writing in last year’s budget document predicted would be spent in 2026.
The new numbers are contained in the much delayed Italian defense budget for 2026, which was sent by the defense ministry to parliament this week for approval.
Defense News has seen the part of the document containing the breakdown on costs per program, but not the section listing total spending.
The GCAP nations in July handed a £4.6 billion ($6.1 billion) development contract to their national champions building the jet after the U.K. freed up delayed cash.
The 18-month contract went to Edgewing, the industrial consortium grouping the firms building the fighter. Germany is reportedly now mulling signing up after the collapse of its plan to build the FCAS jet with France.
The 2026 budget document, which contains spending forecasts, predicts Italy will spend €696 million on the GCAP program in 2027.
Meanwhile spending on heavy army vehicles in 2026 was lower than forecast, despite Italy working on a new main battle tank and fighting vehicle with Rheinmetall.
The program envisages the delivery of 1,050 Lynx vehicles and 272 Panther tanks as part of a €23 billion euro deal. But in July, Italian defense minister Guido Crosetto said Italy would cut 18% in costs from the program.
The new document puts spending on the two new programs, as well as upgrades to Italy’s ageing Ariete tanks, at €177 million in 2026, lower than last year’s €281 million and far lower than the €425 million that last year’s document predicted would be spent in 2026.
By way of compensation, this year’s budget predicts a major hike in spending on the three programs to €872 million in 2027.
Although Defense News has not seen the section of the budget giving total expenditures, a tally of the costs of the individual program outlays this year amounts to €12.8 billion, up by €307 million from the €12.5 billion given by totaling all the programs in the 2025 budget.
Italy’s F-35 program, which involves the eventual purchase of 115 aircraft, cost Italy €782 million in 2026, less than the the €961 million planners last year forecast it would receive.
This year’s budget document has been the focus of heated political debate as defense spending comes under the spotlight ahead of Italian national elections next year, which will see incumbent right wing prime minister Giorgia Meloni seeking reelection.
Meloni’s arguments in favor of defense spending have come under fire from both her allies and foes, including Matteo Salvini, the head of League party which forms part of Meloni’s coalition, and Robert Vannacci, a former army general running a new party to the right of Meloni.
Among opposition parties, the Five Star party has also criticized defense spending, claiming they are diverting scarce funds from health spending.
Students who have recently taken to the streets in Italy as part of a Europe-wide wave of street protests have listed a cut to arms spending as one of their main aims.
The opposition to arms spending has coincided with growing opposition to supplying arms to Ukraine, a policy Meloni has fought for since her election in 2022.

articles.title: US Army names officer held on ‘allegations of espionage’
articles.snippet: Lt. Col. Brandon Carroll Tyner has been identified as the U.S. soldier arrested earlier this week in the UK for reportedly assisting Russian intelligence.
articles.full_text:
An Army official identified Lt. Col. Brandon Carroll Tyner as the U.S. soldier arrested earlier this week in the United Kingdom for reportedly assisting Russian intelligence in what FBI Director Kash Patel described as “allegations of espionage.”
Tyner, 41, began serving in the Army as a human resources officer — military occupational specialty 42H — in January 2008, the official told Military Times. Tyner’s deployments included tours in Afghanistan, Qatar and Iraq.
At the time of his arrest, he was assigned to Imjin Barracks, a British Army base near Gloucestershire, England, which hosts NATO’s Allied Rapid Reaction Corps. His arrest came shortly after the U.S. removed aircraft from British military bases over an unrelated reported threat from Iran.
Tyner was arrested under Sections 1 and 3 of Britain’s 2023 National Security Act and the Army said officials were investigating two locations in Gloucestershire. Counter Terrorism Policing London is leading the investigation and the accused officer remains in custody at a London police station.
“This important arrest involves allegations of espionage, which is of the utmost concern to the United States and our allies,” Patel said in a statement, adding that the FBI had made 167 counterintelligence and espionage arrests over the last 21 months.
Brig. Gen. Sean Stinchon, the commanding general of U.S. Army Counterintelligence Command, thanked the FBI authorities in the UK and encouraged anyone who notices something suspicious to consult officials.
“The alleged conduct of a senior soldier, entrusted with sensitive information, is a sobering reminder that insider threats are real and persistent. I encourage anyone who thinks they’ve witnessed something suspicious to report it to their local counterintelligence office,” he said in a statement.
The arrest comes amid U.S. European Command’s “See Something, Do Something” campaign, which calls on troops, family members and civilian employees to be vigilant about their digital presence and report unusual behavior to authorities. Though the campaign did not identify a specific threat, experts have warned that Russia is ramping up its hybrid warfare.
The Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project, known as ACLED, said in an October report that Russia had increased its hybrid threats across Europe — such as targeting aviation in Germany, attempting to sabotage critical infrastructure in Poland and ramping up drone incursions in Romania and Moldova — in an attempt to weaken the region’s support for Ukraine. The report expects those threats to grow, noting that Moscow would likely use cyberattacks and ramp up attacks against defense and transportation infrastructure.

articles.title: Turkey and Egypt weigh joint naval shipbuilding projects
articles.snippet: Turkey and Egypt are taking steps to strengthen their cooperation in the maritime domain, with joint shipbuilding opportunities on the table.
articles.full_text:
ISTANBUL — Turkey and Egypt are taking steps to strengthen their cooperation in the maritime domain, with joint shipbuilding opportunities on the table.
Adm. Ercüment Tatlıoğlu, the commander of Turkey’s navy, made an announcement to that effect during the Sea of Friendship 2026 naval exercise in Alexandria, Egypt.
The exercise was conducted under the command of Egypt’s Northern Fleet from Nov. 4 to Nov. 9. The previous iteration took place in 2025, following a 13-year hiatus.
The largest warship in the Turkish Navy’s inventory, the amphibious assault ship TCG Anadolu, was among the Turkish units participating in the exercise. The drill covered surface warfare, anti-submarine warfare, air defense operations and underwater assault training.
Tatlıoğlu held talks with his Egyptian counterpart, Vice Adm. Mahmoud Adel Fawzy, on the sidelines of the event at Alexandria Naval Base on Nov. 7.
Tatlıoğlu described the Sea of Friendship exercise as a substantial demonstration of growing cooperation between Turkey and Egypt in the Eastern Mediterranean. He said the two navies were taking concrete steps to expand cooperation in unmanned aerial and naval systems, highlighting the participation of the Bayraktar TB3 unmanned aerial vehicle and the MKE Pirana one-way unmanned surface vehicle.
“We aim to take our defense industry cooperation in the maritime domain to a more advanced level by undertaking joint shipbuilding activities with Egypt, similar to the cooperation we have established with Pakistan under the MILGEM Project,” Tatlıoğlu said.
The MILGEM Project was initiated by the Turkish Navy to design and build indigenously developed naval platforms. The project has resulted in the development of Ada-class corvettes and Istanbul-class frigates, which are in service with the Turkish Navy, as well as Ada-class variants for the Pakistani, Ukrainian and Malaysian navies and a Hisar-class offshore patrol vessel for the Romanian Navy.
Meanwhile, Fawzy described this month’s exercise as well planned and executed despite sea conditions that were not particularly favorable.
“This activity demonstrates that we are on the right track,” he said. “We can train together, plan together and conduct ship-boarding activities together. We can work together. In the near future, the Egyptian and Turkish navies may be able to operate side by side, shoulder to shoulder, on joint missions.”
The naval exercise took place just 15 days after the House of Representatives in eastern Libya, based in Benghazi, unanimously ratified a Turkey–Libya maritime jurisdiction agreement on Oct 20.
The original 2019 Turkey-Libya maritime delimitation agreement is strategically important as it establishes a boundary between the two countries’ claimed continental shelves and exclusive economic zones (EEZs) in the Eastern Mediterranean.
For Turkey, this agreement is to protect its maritime jurisdiction claims and prevent Greek islands from effectively limiting Turkey’s access to maritime areas. For Libya, it provides a basis for asserting its own maritime rights.
Greece opposes the agreement, arguing that it disregards the maritime entitlements of Greek islands and undermines its claims in the Eastern Mediterranean.
In 2019, the agreement was signed only by Libya’s Government of National Accord in Tripoli. Now it has been ratified by the House of Representatives in Benghazi, thus bringing the two major parties in Libya to accept the agreement.
Even so, Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty described the pact as “completely null and void” during an Oct. 23 visit to Istanbul, where he met his Turkish counterpart, Hakan Fidan.
Serhat Güvenç, a professor of international relations at Kadir Has University in Istanbul, stated that Egypt was still unwilling to sign an agreement on exclusive economic zones (EEZs) with Turkey but was, at the same time, cooperating with Turkey in a major naval exercise in which TCG Anadolu was also participating.
“Egypt’s position regarding the Memorandum of Understanding signed with Libya and its willingness to develop military and maritime relations with Türkiye are not mutually exclusive,” he said. “In fact, in this picture, Egypt may perhaps be in a better position than the other actors in terms of respect for international law and acting with due care in this regard, because Turkey and Greece are pursuing maximalist positions.”

articles.title: Democrats push to remove US-Israel tech measure from defense bill
articles.snippet: The measures call for enhanced cooperation between the U.S. and Israel on weapons technology development.
articles.full_text:
Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., is leading a push to remove provisions from the Senate and House versions of this year’s National Defense Authorization Act that would promote closer ties between the U.S. industrial base and Israel’s.
A letter sent Tuesday to House and Senate leadership signed by Van Hollen and 11 other Senate colleagues, including Sens. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Tammy Duckworth, D-Ill., specifically addresses Section 1217 of the Senate version and Section 219 of the House version of the bill.
Those sections, called the United States-Israel Defense Cooperation Initiative in the House and the United States-Israel Framework for Upgraded Technologies, Unified Research, and Enhanced Security (FUTURES) Act in the Senate, each call for enhanced cooperation between the two countries on weapons technology development, including in artificial intelligence, quantum technology and chemical and biological weapons.
“The Senator is working with his colleagues to remove these provisions and will determine next steps should they remain in,” Van Hollen’s office said in an email to Military Times. “The Senator will continue to push to remove these provisions and push to protect the United States’ ability to act independently and in line with U.S. national security interests.”
The letter also addresses a provision of the fiscal 2027 Intelligence Authorization Act that proposes enhancing intelligence-sharing between the two countries, which, according to the text of the bill, is intended to help Israel “maintain its qualitative military edge” and “deter and counter destabilizing activities by the Government of Iran and Iran-aligned state and nonstate actors that threaten Israel, United States forces, and regional partners.”
The U.S. government’s support for Israel has come under intense scrutiny over the past three years. Israel’s war in Gaza has killed at least 74,000 Palestinians, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry, and U.S. and Israeli attacks against Iran on Feb. 28 led to a war that’s increasingly unpopular in the United States, a new Reuters/Ipsos poll found.
President Donald Trump promised to end outright military aid to Israel, which has previously come via a Memorandum of Understanding. The current MOU is set to expire in 2028 and provides billions in financing for Israel to procure U.S.-made weapons over the 10-year agreement.
Critics, including Van Hollen, have noted that the annual defense bills, as they stand, merely shift military provision from an aid model to a commercial partnership, this time overseen by the Pentagon rather than the State Department.
The new model, as proposed in the draft legislation, “would constrain the administration’s ability to independently determine how best to protect U.S. national security and would lock in long-term commitments despite our serious concerns with the Israeli government’s actions in Gaza, the West Bank, and other parts of the region,” the letter states.
The U.S. and Israel already cooperate on some defense technology; Israeli contractor Rafael Systems and Raytheon developed the David’s Sling missile interceptor system. But critics say that the proposed setup would decrease oversight of the weapons transfer system; could compromise sensitive U.S. weapons technology; and wouldn’t provide much benefit for the United States.
The NDAA is one of Congress’s “must-pass” bills, but the price tag alone — more than $1 trillion — has drawn significant pushback from Democrats. The House’s version narrowly passed in July, and Senate Democrats blocked that chamber’s version the same month, objecting to provisions for the Iran war.
In the House, Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., tried unsuccessfully to pass an amendment striking the United States-Israel Defense Cooperation Initiative when the bill was being debated in committee. Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., was also a vocal opponent.

articles.title: Hermeus recruits Northrop Grumman to Quarterhorse drone program
articles.snippet: The defense giant will supply mission systems for Hermeus’ Quarterhorse unmanned aircraft, adding a new partner among a team of industry heavyweights.
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON — Northrop Grumman is partnering with Hermeus to supply mission systems for the startup’s aircraft, adding another industry player to the team as Hermeus pushes to field a high-speed drone.
In a press release published Thursday, Hermeus said Northrop will provide “integrated mission systems design, development, integration, and sustainment” for Hermeus’ aircraft. The partnership “creates a path to equip Hermeus’ aircraft with technology across sensing, communications, navigation, and command and control, allowing the aircraft to operate more intelligently and take on more complex missions,” the release adds.
“We’re building a new class of aircraft that gives the warfighter improved speed, range, and flexibility while integrating into the existing Force,” Hermeus CEO Zach Shore said in the company’s release. “Adding Northrop Grumman’s battle-tested mission systems will push what those aircraft can do in real world scenarios and help us field operational capability faster.”
Founded in 2018, Hermeus is currently developing its Quarterhorse drone with funding from the Pentagon’s Defense Innovation Unit. Military officials have expressed strong interest in the platform, which the company is pushing to fly at speeds as fast as Mach 3 through an iterative design process. The drone achieved supersonic flight earlier this year.
Northrop is a key supplier of mission systems across the defense industrial base, including radars, electronic warfare kits and navigation equipment for US military platforms.
In a separate release, Northrop said it will integrate its mission systems onto the Quarterhorse. Northrop Program Manager Kyle Mimken told Breaking Defense in a statement that “at a high level,” the company will bring “electronic warfare, communications, sensing and navigation along with the payload-integration and systems-engineering experience needed to make those capabilities work together on an aircraft.”
Mimken declined to comment on which specific systems the company plans to integrate, but stressed that Northrop’s contributions will help make the aircraft more survivable and effective. He added that the partnership’s “immediate focus” is mission systems integration and coordinating with Hermeus to prepare for flight testing.
From directed energy to AI and hardening, JIATF-401 is widening counter-UAS options
There is no single answer to the drone threat, pushing the Pentagon toward a broader mix of defenses.
“We expect to begin trials of elements of our mission-system kit in our testing environments in the summer,” Mimken said.
Northrop’s addition marks another industry heavyweight on the Quarterhorse team. In September, Hermeus revealed that it will use autonomy software supplied by defense tech firm Anduril for upcoming flight tests.
The Quarterhorse is powered by Pratt & Whitney’s F100 fighter jet engine. Shortly after announcing the Anduril partnership, Hermeus executives told Breaking Defense that the company had reached an agreement with Pratt to manufacture the F100 under license — the first such deal for an American firm. Hermeus officials believe the arrangement positions the company to be virtually the only vertically integrated planemaker in the business.
Hermeus is also building its own turbine-based combined cycle (TBCC) engine based on the F100. A TBCC engine combines a jet turbine with a ramjet engine to create an integrated propulsion system capable of pushing an aircraft to hypersonic speeds exceeding Mach 5. articles.title: UK to buy three new mine-hunting drone motherships under Norway agreement
articles.snippet: The decision, for which £90 million ($119.1 million) has been allocated, was formalized on Thursday by British Defense Secretary Wes Streeting and his Norwegian counterpart, Tore O. Sandvik, at the Atlantic Future Forum in Oslo.
articles.full_text:
MILAN — The UK this week formalized plans to purchase three new mine-hunting “motherships” that can deploy unmanned mine countermeasure assets, as part of a defense cooperation agreement with Norway.
Under the UK-Norway Lunna House Agreement, signed last December, the British government announced its intention to join the Norwegian P1118 Standardized Vessel Program to develop offshore support vessels as motherships for autonomous mine-hunting systems.
The decision, for which £90 million ($119.1 million) has been allocated, was formalized on Thursday by British Defense Secretary Wes Streeting and his Norwegian counterpart, Tore O. Sandvik, at the Atlantic Future Forum in Oslo.
“This deal strengthens our ability to protect freedom of navigation, which is critical to our security and our economy …[We are] using the biggest sustained increase in defense spending since the Cold War to put the latest modern technology in the hands of our sailors,” Streeting said.
The British Ministry of Defense said the vessels, built on the same family as Norway’s naval version of the P1118 design, will help keep sailors “further from danger” and, as a result, support “anti-submarine warfare capabilities on NATO’s northern flank.”
The first ship is expected to arrive in 2031, and the deal includes an option for London to order three more.
The threat posed by naval mines, especially in the Strait of Hormuz, has surged since the start of the Iran war in February, when Tehran launched mine-laying operations to restrict navigation of the waterway. In Thursday’s announcement, the British MoD called these operations “illegal.” It said they caused “major disruption to the global trade in energy,” adding that the new mine-hunting capabilities will help the UK stay ahead of this threat.
